note: An extract, not the series. For each observation, its first published value and each value it changed to, with the vintage that changed it. The basis column carries the series title at that vintage, which is where the base year lives: a rebasing changes every value and revises none of them.

series.name: IHYQ
series.label: Gross Domestic Product: quarter on quarter growth
series.units: per cent, chained volume measure, seasonally adjusted
series.why: GDP quarter on quarter growth. A rate, so it has no base to move: every difference between two vintages is a genuine revision. The headline series.
distinct_bases: Gross Domestic Product: Quarter on Quarter growth: CVM SA %

series.name: MGSX
series.label: Unemployment rate, aged 16 and over
series.why: Unemployment rate. Also a rate, and revised far less often than GDP, which makes it the control: a corpus where everything moves cannot show that an agent knows when something did not.
distinct_bases: LFS: Unemployment rate: UK: All: Aged 16 and over: %: SA
Unemployment rate (aged 16 and over, seasonally adjusted)
Unemployment rate (aged 16 and over, seasonally adjusted): %

series.name: ABMI
series.label: Gross Domestic Product: chained volume measure
series.why: Real GDP as a level, in chained volume measures. Re-referenced over the period, so almost every value differs from its first published form without most of them having been revised. Here to be told apart from IHYQ.
distinct_bases: Gross Domestic Product: chained volume measures: Seasonally adjusted £m

series.name: D7BT
series.label: Consumer prices index: all items
series.units: index, and the base year is in the basis column because it moved
series.why: CPI index. Rebased from 2005=100 to 2015=100 inside the window, which is the cleanest example in the corpus of a change that looks like a revision and is not.
distinct_bases: CPI All Items Index: Estimated pre-97 2005=100
CPI All Items Index: Estimated pre-97 2015=100
